title: The Rainhill Trials and the Rocket
summary: In 1829 a railway company held a race to find the best engine, and thousands of people came to watch. A horse on a treadmill, a speedy little engine called Novelty and a few others all broke down or dropped out. Only one locomotive, the yellow-and-black Rocket, finished every test and won the prize.

sections.heading: A Railway That Might Not Have Used Locomotives
paragraphs: By the spring of 1829, a brand-new railway was creeping across the countryside of north-west England. It would link Liverpool, the great port where ships brought in raw cotton from across the Atlantic, with Manchester, the booming factory town about 30 miles inland where that cotton was spun and woven into cloth. Merchants had grown tired of paying high prices to the canal companies, whose barges were slow and whose owners knew they had little competition. A railway, they hoped, would be faster and cheaper. George Stephenson, fresh from the Stockton and Darlington, had been hired as its engineer.

But there was one enormous question that nobody had yet settled. What would actually pull the trains? Today that sounds like a silly question, because of course trains have locomotives. In 1829 it was not silly at all. Locomotives were still new, rare and unreliable. The few that existed in the coalfields broke down often, rattled along at a walking pace, and sometimes damaged the track. Many sensible engineers thought they were an interesting toy that would never be trusted with a busy main line.

There was a serious rival idea: stationary engines. Instead of putting a steam engine on wheels, you could build big steam engines in engine houses beside the line, every mile or two. Each engine would turn a huge drum that wound in a long rope or chain, and that rope would haul the wagons along to the next engine house, where they would be handed on to the next rope, like a relay race. This was called cable haulage, and it was a proven technology. Stationary engines had been hauling coal wagons up slopes for years, including on the Stockton and Darlington itself. On the Hetton colliery line in County Durham, which Stephenson himself had built, stationary engines and ropes did much of the hauling over the hills.

The directors of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway were split. Some backed Stephenson, who was absolutely certain that the moving locomotive was the future. Others worried that locomotives were too weak and too unreliable, and that the public was frightened of them. While the company had been asking Parliament for permission to build the line, it had quietly played down the idea of steam locomotives, because so many landowners and townspeople were alarmed by the thought of fire-breathing machines rushing past their homes.

To help them decide, the directors asked two experienced engineers, James Walker and John Urpeth Rastrick, to visit the railways of the north-east and report back. Their report, delivered in early 1829, did not give the clear victory Stephenson wanted. It weighed up costs and suggested that stationary engines might do the job well, though locomotives might improve in future. Stephenson argued back fiercely. A cable system, he pointed out, had a fatal weakness: if one engine or one rope failed, the whole line stopped, like a chain of people passing buckets where one person drops out. A locomotive that broke down could simply be replaced by another.

So the directors came up with a bold and very public solution. They would hold a competition. If inventors believed a locomotive could do the job, let them build one and prove it on the line, in front of judges and the whole watching world.

sections.heading: The Rules of the Great Contest
paragraphs: In April 1829 the directors announced a prize of 500 pounds for the best locomotive that met their conditions. That was a lot of money, roughly the cost of a substantial house at the time, and many tens of thousands of pounds in today's money. Even more valuable than the prize was what it might lead to: the winner could expect orders for many more engines from the railway.

The rules were strict, because the directors wanted a machine that could do real, everyday work, not just put on a show. Here are the main ones, as reported in accounts of the trials. The engine had to burn its own smoke, so it would not cover the countryside in soot; in practice this meant burning coke, a cleaner fuel made by baking coal. Its boiler pressure must not be more than 50 pounds per square inch, and it had to have two safety valves, one of which the driver could not tamper with. It had to stand on springs, and it could weigh no more than six tons, or four and a half tons if it ran on only four wheels. The finished engine had to cost no more than 550 pounds.

Then came the test itself. A flat, straight stretch of the new line at Rainhill, roughly 9 or 10 miles east of Liverpool, was chosen as the race track. Each engine would be weighed and then given a load of wagons equal to three times its own weight, counting its tender. It had to start with a cold boiler and no fire, so the judges could see how quickly it raised steam. Then it had to run up and down a measured course of one and three-quarter miles, which included an eighth of a mile at each end for speeding up and slowing down.

Ten trips made 35 miles, a little more than the distance from Liverpool to Manchester. The engine had to average at least 10 miles per hour. After the first ten trips it could stop to take on fuel and water, and then it had to do another ten trips, for a total of 70 miles. In other words, the directors were asking each engine to prove it could make a return journey between the two cities, pulling a heavy load, without falling to pieces.

Three judges would watch everything and record the times, the fuel used and the water used. They were John Rastrick, one of the authors of the report that had favoured stationary engines; Nicholas Wood, a mining engineer from Killingworth who knew Stephenson's early locomotives well; and John Kennedy, a Manchester cotton spinner who supported the railway. It was a fair mix: one doubter, one expert, and one businessman.

sections.heading: A Day Out at Rainhill
paragraphs: Imagine standing on a grassy bank beside the line at Rainhill on Tuesday 6 October 1829. It is a cool autumn morning. Thousands of people have come from Liverpool, Manchester and the villages around, by carriage, on horseback and on foot. Some estimates put the crowd at between 10,000 and 15,000 people over the most popular days. Grandstands have been put up for ladies and gentlemen. A band is playing. Men in top hats peer through telescopes, and engineers scribble figures in notebooks. Children perch on their fathers' shoulders to get a better view.

Many in the crowd have never seen a locomotive before. Newspapers have been printing stories about the contest for weeks, and reporters from London and abroad are there. Nobody quite knows what will happen. Will the engines explode? Will they work at all? Will a horse-drawn coach still be faster? It is part science experiment, part sporting event and part fairground.

The trials were supposed to last a few days, but breakdowns, repairs and arguments stretched them out from 6 to 14 October. Ten machines had been entered in all, but only five were ready to compete when the contest opened. Some never left their workshops. One was a carriage powered by two men, which plainly could not meet the rules. The five that did arrive were very different from one another, and each told a story about the different ideas engineers had about how a locomotive should be built.

sections.heading: Meet the Contestants
paragraphs: Rocket came from Newcastle upon Tyne, built at Robert Stephenson and Company, the locomotive factory the Stephensons had set up in 1823. It was a small, bright machine painted yellow and black, with a tall white chimney at the front and a barrel-shaped boiler lying behind it. Two cylinders were mounted on its sides at a steep angle, driving one pair of large front wheels, each about 4 feet 8 and a half inches across, with a pair of small wheels at the back. It weighed only about four and a quarter tons. To reach Rainhill, it was carried in pieces by horse-drawn wagons across northern England to Carlisle, then shipped down the coast to Liverpool and put back together.

Novelty was the surprise of the contest. It was built in London in a hurry by John Braithwaite, an engineer who made fire engines, and John Ericsson, a brilliant young Swedish inventor. It looked more like a neat little cart than an iron horse. It carried its water in a tank on its own frame instead of in a separate tender, which makes it the first known tank locomotive. Instead of a tall chimney, it used bellows, worked by the engine itself, to blow air into its fire. It was light, low and handsome, and the crowd loved it at once. Ericsson later moved to the United States, where he designed the famous ironclad warship USS Monitor during the American Civil War.

Sans Pareil, French for 'without equal', was built by Timothy Hackworth, the experienced locomotive superintendent of the Stockton and Darlington Railway. Hackworth had helped build Puffing Billy years before and knew more about running locomotives every day than almost anyone. His engine was sturdy and powerful, with a boiler in which the fire's hot gases travelled along a U-shaped flue, there and back, before escaping up the chimney. It was built at the Stockton and Darlington's workshops at Shildon, in whatever spare time Hackworth had, and some of its parts were made by outside firms, including, as it happened, Robert Stephenson and Company.

Perseverance was built by Timothy Burstall of Edinburgh. It had an upright boiler and was more like a steam road carriage than a railway engine. Sadly for Burstall, it was damaged on the long journey from Scotland to Rainhill, and he spent the first days of the trials repairing it.

Cycloped was the strangest of all. Built by Thomas Shaw Brandreth of Liverpool, it was not a steam engine at all. A horse stood on a moving platform, a kind of treadmill made from a belt, inside the machine. As the horse walked, the belt turned, and gears passed that motion to the wheels. It was a clever idea, but it broke the spirit of the contest, which was meant to find a locomotive engine. It did not last long either: during one run the horse burst through the floor of the machine, and Cycloped became the first entry to drop out.

sections.heading: Nine Days of Drama
paragraphs: Rocket was ready first and set the standard. Over the days of the trials it ran its first set of trips at a steady pace and then, after refuelling, its second set, averaging roughly 12 miles per hour including all the stops and starts at each end of the course. That comfortably beat the required 10 miles per hour. On its fastest stretches it reached about 30 miles per hour, and when it was running without its load of wagons, it was reported going even faster. Most people in 1829 had never travelled faster than a galloping horse. To see a machine do it, all by itself, was astonishing.

Rocket's careful records impressed the judges as much as its speed. A report in The Times said it covered its first 35 miles in about 3 hours 10 minutes and the second 35 miles in about 2 hours 52 minutes, burning less than half a ton of coke over the whole 70 miles. It did not break down once. Between runs, the Stephensons even gave the crowd a show, sending Rocket back and forth along the line with a carriage full of passengers.

Novelty was the crowd's darling. On its first runs it shot along at about 28 miles per hour, faster than anything people had seen, and many spectators were sure it would win. But it was not built for hard, long work. A pipe in its boiler failed. Braithwaite and Ericsson worked through the night to repair it, and Novelty ran again, but more failures followed, including trouble with its bellows and boiler joints, and in the end it had to be withdrawn. Its light, clever design had simply not been tested enough before the great day.

Sans Pareil had trouble before it even started. When it was weighed, it turned out to be over the weight limit, by about 300 pounds (about 140 kilograms). The judges allowed it to run anyway, but made it clear it could not win the prize. It completed eight of its trips, burning a great deal of fuel, until one of its cylinders cracked and it had to stop. Hackworth was bitterly disappointed, and some of his supporters later claimed that the cracked cylinder was poor work by the Stephensons' factory, which had cast it. Historians cannot prove this either way.

Perseverance, after Burstall's days of repairs, finally ran on the sixth day, but it could only manage about 5 or 6 miles per hour, well short of the target. Burstall withdrew. The judges were kind enough to award him 25 pounds for his efforts, a consolation prize for perseverance indeed.

So when the dust settled on 14 October 1829, only one engine had done everything the rules asked: Rocket. The judges declared it the winner. Shortly afterwards it went on to show it could climb too, pulling loaded wagons up the slope at Whiston near Rainhill, which helped answer critics who said locomotives could only work on flat ground.

sections.heading: Inside Rocket: Three Clever Ideas
paragraphs: Why did Rocket succeed where the others failed? It was not because it was the most powerful engine ever built. Rather, it combined three good ideas in one small, light machine, and those ideas fitted together so well that they became the basic recipe for steam locomotives for the next 130 years.

The first idea was the multi-tubular boiler. Earlier locomotives, like Puffing Billy and Locomotion, used a boiler with one or two big flues, wide pipes that carried the hot gases from the fire through the water. Think of trying to warm a bath with one hot pipe running through it. Only the water touching the pipe gets heated quickly. Rocket's boiler, about 6 feet long and a little over 3 feet across, had 25 narrow copper tubes, each about 3 inches wide, running from end to end. The hot gases from the fire rushed through all 25 tubes at once. Because there were so many tubes, the total hot surface touching the water was much bigger, so the boiler could turn water into steam far faster. More steam, more power, for a boiler that was still small enough for a light engine to carry.

The second idea was the separate firebox. Rocket's fire burned in its own box at the back, bolted onto the end of the boiler. The firebox had double walls with water between them, a 'water jacket'. This meant the heat glowing out from the burning coke warmed the water in the jacket directly, instead of being wasted, and the walls of the firebox were kept cool enough not to burn through. The burning gases then left the firebox and entered the tubes.

The third idea was the blastpipe. When steam had done its job pushing the pistons, it was not simply let out into the air. Instead, a pipe directed this used, or exhaust, steam straight up the chimney in sharp puffs. Each puff dragged air up the chimney behind it, which pulled fresh air in through the fire grate, just like blowing on a campfire makes it blaze. The faster Rocket ran, the more often it puffed, and the harder its fire burned, so it automatically made more steam exactly when it needed it most. This is also where the famous 'chuff, chuff' sound of a steam train comes from.

There was a clever partnership between these ideas. A strong blast through a single big flue could suck the fire out of the chimney as sparks and waste. But a blast pulling through 25 narrow tubes was evened out, drawing the fire hard without throwing it away. The tubes needed the blast, and the blast worked best with the tubes.

Rocket also had cylinders that drove the wheels directly by rods, with no gears, and it sat on springs for a smoother ride. Its cylinders at first sloped at a steep angle of about 38 degrees, which made it rock as it ran. Within a year or two, engineers lowered them to almost horizontal, a layout that later locomotives followed.

sections.heading: Who Really Designed Rocket?
paragraphs: It is often called 'Stephenson's Rocket', and many people imagine George Stephenson designing it alone. The real story is more interesting, and fairer to several people.

In 1829 George was extremely busy acting as chief engineer of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, overseeing tunnels, cuttings and bridges on the line. The daily work of designing and building Rocket happened in Newcastle under his son, Robert Stephenson, who was only 25 years old. Robert had trained as an engineer, studied for a time at the University of Edinburgh, and spent three years working on mines in South America before coming home to run the factory. Father and son wrote to each other often, and George surely gave advice, but most historians agree that Robert deserves the credit for most of Rocket's design and for solving the many practical problems of building it.

The idea of using many small tubes in the boiler was suggested to the Stephensons by Henry Booth, the treasurer of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway. Booth was not a trained engineer, but he was a thoughtful, inventive man. He became a partner in the entry, and when Rocket won, the prize money was shared between Booth and the Stephensons. At almost the same time, a French engineer named Marc Seguin was building locomotives with multi-tube boilers for a railway near Lyon in France, so the idea was 'in the air' in more than one country.

The blastpipe also had a longer history. Richard Trevithick had noticed back in 1804 that turning his engine's exhaust steam up the chimney made the fire burn more fiercely. George Stephenson used exhaust steam in the chimney on his early colliery engines, and Timothy Hackworth also used a strong blastpipe, including on Sans Pareil. Who 'invented' it is still argued about. What Rocket did was combine the blastpipe with the multi-tube boiler so that each made the other work better.

This is how most great inventions really happen. One person rarely creates everything. Instead, a team brings together ideas, some new and some borrowed or improved, and builds them into something that works better than any of the parts alone.

sections.heading: Victory, and What Happened to Rocket
paragraphs: Rainhill settled the great argument. The directors of the Liverpool and Manchester Railway dropped the idea of stationary engines and ropes for the main line. Locomotives would pull their trains, and Robert Stephenson and Company won the contract to build them. The railway even bought Sans Pareil from Hackworth, and it worked for them for a couple of years before being hired out to another line.

Rocket was soon put to work. Just after Christmas, on 28 December 1829, it carried about 40 passengers across the newly finished section over the bog of Chat Moss, a crossing you will read about in the next part. But locomotive design was racing ahead. Within a year, Robert Stephenson's factory was building bigger and better engines, such as Northumbrian and Planet, and Rocket was soon rebuilt and left behind. After working on the Liverpool and Manchester for a few years, it was sold in 1837 to a small coal railway near Brampton in Cumberland, in the far north of England, and was laid aside around 1840 as too light for heavy mineral trains.

Happily, it was not scrapped. In 1862 its owners gave what remained of Rocket to the Patent Office Museum in London, which later became the Science Museum. It stayed there for about 150 years, battered and incomplete but treasured, seen by millions of visitors. In 2018 and 2019 it made a tour of the north, including a visit to Manchester, close to the old Liverpool Road station where its railway once ended, and it is now cared for at the National Railway Museum in York. Working replicas built in 1979 still give rides today, so people can hear what that first winning 'chuff' sounded like.

But in the autumn of 1830, Rocket was not yet a museum piece. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway was almost finished, and an opening ceremony was being planned, grander than anything the railway world had seen. The Prime Minister himself, the Duke of Wellington, was coming. Rocket was being polished and prepared to take its place in the great procession of engines on 15 September 1830, a day that would bring triumph to the railway, and also tragedy.

deepDive: Rainhill is often told as a simple race, but historians see it as a carefully designed engineering trial, and a political one. The Walker and Rastrick report of 1829 had compared the costs of locomotives and fixed engines with ropes and judged the question still open; the directors used the trials partly to win over doubters on their own board and in the public. The rules, with a load of three times the engine's weight, a cold start, limits on pressure and weight, and a 70-mile endurance test, rewarded reliability and fuel economy more than raw speed. That is why Novelty, the fastest engine on its first day, did not win. A 2002 restaging with replicas, shown in a 2003 BBC Timewatch programme, found Novelty and Sans Pareil each failed about half their runs, while calculations suggested Rocket would still have come out ahead. Experiments showed that Novelty's fire could become choked by clinker, the melted ash that forms when coke burns very hot. The science of Rocket's success lies in heat transfer. Rocket's heating surface was about 15 square metres, of which the 25 tubes supplied about 13. Spreading the hot gas through many narrow tubes greatly increases the area of metal that passes heat into the water, and the blastpipe increases the rate at which air is drawn through the fire. The result is that steam production rises naturally with speed, a self-regulating loop that remained the heart of steam locomotive design until the end of steam. There are still lively debates about credit. Robert Stephenson led the design, Henry Booth proposed the tubes, Marc Seguin was developing multi-tubular boilers in France at the same time, and claims for the blastpipe go back to Trevithick, George Stephenson and Hackworth. Supporters of Hackworth also argued that his cylinder failure came from a faulty casting supplied by the Stephensons' own factory, a claim that cannot now be proved. Finally, Rocket itself was a short-lived design. It was rebuilt within about 18 months, and later engines such as Planet, with horizontal cylinders under the smokebox, became the real pattern for the future.
funFact: Rocket's single pair of driving wheels were 4 feet 8 and a half inches across, exactly the same as the width of the standard gauge track it ran on.
